value.overview: The Wood Thrush (Hylocichla mustelina) is a medium-sized North American songbird known for its rich, flute-like song and boldly spotted white underparts. It breeds in mature and regenerating deciduous forests of the United States and southern Canada, then migrates to wooded areas of Central America. Costa Rica is an important wintering and migration country for the species. Although still widespread, Wood Thrush numbers have declined substantially because of habitat loss, forest fragmentation, and other pressures.
value.classification: The Wood Thrush belongs to the thrush family, Turdidae, within the order Passeriformes. It is the only living species in the genus Hylocichla.
value.identification: Adults have warm cinnamon-brown upperparts, a white breast and belly covered with large dark spots, and a rounded body with a relatively large head. The back is generally brighter reddish-brown than the head and tail. The sexes look alike. Its upright posture, deliberate movements on the forest floor, and habit of turning leaves while feeding are useful field marks. The song is distinctive: a series of clear, musical phrases, often ending in a soft, echoing note.
value.rangeHabitat: The Wood Thrush breeds across much of the eastern United States and southeastern Canada, especially in mature deciduous and mixed forests with a leafy understory. During the nonbreeding season it occurs from Mexico through Central America to Panama and northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica, it is a regular winter visitor and migrant, generally present from about October through April. It uses forest interiors, humid foothill and lowland woodland, forest edges, shaded plantations, and other habitats with dense vegetation and leaf litter.
value.migrationStatus: The Wood Thrush is a long-distance migrant. Most birds leave the breeding range in late summer and autumn, cross the Gulf of Mexico or travel around it, and winter in Central America. In Costa Rica it is primarily a regular migrant and winter resident from approximately October to April, rather than a breeding species.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs from April through August, with timing varying by latitude. The female builds a cup-shaped nest of leaves, grasses, and plant fibers, commonly placed on a horizontal branch in a shrub or tree. A typical clutch contains two to four pale blue eggs. Both adults feed the nestlings, and pairs may attempt more than one brood. Nest success can be reduced in fragmented forests by predators and Brown-headed Cowbird brood parasitism.
value.dietFeeding: The Wood Thrush feeds mainly on insects and other invertebrates during the breeding season, including beetles, caterpillars, ants, and other arthropods. In autumn and winter it consumes more fruit, especially berries from forest plants and shrubs. It commonly forages alone or in loose association with other birds, searching through leaf litter and low vegetation. It may hop, pause upright, and probe or flip leaves to uncover prey.
value.behavior: This species is often secretive, remaining beneath trees and shrubs rather than staying in exposed places. It usually forages on the ground and may defend a breeding territory with song. Wood Thrushes are generally solitary during breeding but can gather at productive fruiting plants during migration or winter. Males sing from elevated perches, especially early in the morning, and the species is capable of remarkable nocturnal migration over long distances.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is declining. Long-term monitoring in North America has recorded substantial reductions since the late twentieth century, although trends vary among regions. Wintering populations in Central America, including Costa Rica, depend on the continued availability and quality of forest habitat.
conservation.threats: Major threats include loss and fragmentation of mature forest on the breeding grounds and in Central America, degradation of wintering habitat, collisions with buildings during migration, nest predation, and brood parasitism by Brown-headed Cowbirds. Climate change may also alter food availability, migration timing, and suitable habitat. Deforestation in the species’ Central American wintering range is especially important because many birds concentrate in relatively limited forest areas.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mature and regenerating forests, forest corridors, and shaded, structurally diverse habitat in both breeding and wintering regions. In Costa Rica, conserving lowland and foothill forests, reforestation areas, and connected woodland can support wintering birds. Reduce window collisions by applying effective bird-safe window treatments, keep cats indoors, and support monitoring and habitat-protection programs for migratory landbirds.
